etymology: Hermann Wits, latinized Witsius (1636-1708); the Dutch Reformed theologian and covenant divine, author of The Economy of the Covenants Between God and Man.
biblical_def: Herman Witsius (1636-1708) was a Dutch Reformed theologian and one of the great covenant divines, best remembered for his masterwork The Economy of the Covenants Between God and Man, a full and irenic exposition of the covenant of works and the covenant of grace. Learned, devout, and peaceable, he laboured to set forth the biblical covenants in their order and harmony, holding together the doctrines of grace with a warm experimental piety, and seeking to reconcile the more scholastic and the more pietistic strains of Reformed divinity in his day. The dictionary honours Witsius as a faithful expositor of covenant theology, which reads the whole of Scripture through the covenants God has made: the covenant of works with Adam, broken in the fall; and the covenant of grace in Christ, the second Adam, by which God promised, “I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed… to be a God unto thee.” This is the better covenant of which Christ is mediator, established upon better promises, the covenant under which God writes His law in the inward parts. Witsius rightly divided the word of truth, a workman approved unto God. The dictionary commends him as a model of Reformed covenant theology pursued with both precision and devotion—learning that warmed rather than chilled the heart—and as a witness that doctrinal exactness and experimental godliness are not rivals but companions. His Economy of the Covenants remains a standard exposition of the covenantal framework the Reformed tradition reads across the unity of Scripture, from the first Adam to the last.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle Witsius commends is the union of doctrinal precision and experimental godliness. A persistent error pits the two against each other—treating careful theology as cold and deadening, and warm piety as careless of doctrine. Witsius refutes the divorce. He was at once a precise covenant scholar and a man of devout, heartfelt religion, and he laboured to reconcile the scholastic and pietistic strains of the Reformed church of his day. The dictionary holds, with his example, that learning ought to warm the heart and that true devotion is built on sound doctrine.

Witsius also commends covenant theology itself as the framework for reading the unity of Scripture. The Bible is not a heap of disconnected stories but the unfolding of God's covenants—the covenant of works with Adam, broken in the fall, and the covenant of grace in Christ the last Adam, the better covenant established upon better promises. The dictionary commends Witsius as a faithful guide to this covenantal reading, and his Economy of the Covenants as a standard exposition, honouring him as a workman approved unto God who rightly divided the word of truth with both exactness and warmth.

etymology: From “founders,” the original framers of the Southern Baptist Convention; the ministry that calls Baptists back to the doctrines of grace held by their founders.
biblical_def: Founders Ministries is a movement and ministry, arising in the early 1980s, that calls Baptists—and Southern Baptists in particular—back to the doctrines of grace and the confessional, Reformed convictions held by the founders of the Southern Baptist Convention and the wider Particular Baptist tradition. Its name presses the historical claim that the early Southern Baptists were largely Calvinistic, framing their work on the doctrines of grace and the Second London (1689) and Abstract of Principles confessions, and that the later drift toward decisional revivalism and Arminian method was a departure from those roots. The dictionary, standing in the Reformed Baptist tradition, commends the aim of Founders: to recover the doctrines of grace, confessional integrity, and the old paths among Baptists, contending earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints, holding fast the form of sound words, and asking for the old paths, the good way, that the churches might find rest for their souls. Their convictions rest on the one foundation: other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ. The dictionary marks the movement as a genuine work of recovery, while noting—as with any contemporary ministry—that it is to be judged not by its name or reputation but by its fidelity to Scripture and the confession. Founders' abiding value is the reminder that confessional Calvinism is not a novelty among Baptists but their heritage, and that reformation in a denomination comes by returning to the doctrines of grace and the sound words handed down, not by chasing the methods and measures of the age.

etymology: From Psalm 60:4, “a banner… because of the truth”; the Banner of Truth Trust, a Reformed publishing ministry founded in 1957 to republish the Puritans and Reformed classics.
biblical_def: The Banner of Truth Trust is a Reformed publishing ministry, founded in Britain in 1957, devoted to republishing the works of the Puritans, the Reformers, and the great Reformed and experimental divines, together with sound contemporary literature, for the recovery of doctrinal and experimental Christianity. Its name is taken from the Psalm: “Thou hast given a banner to them that fear thee, that it may be displayed because of the truth.” The dictionary honours the Banner of Truth as a chief instrument, under God, of the twentieth-century recovery of Reformed and Puritan literature, putting back into the hands of pastors and people the writings of Owen, Bunyan, the Westminster divines, the Scottish and English Puritans, and the Reformers—treasures long out of print. By such republishing it has served the church's sanctification through the truth, for the Lord prayed, “Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth,” and the apostle charged that the sound words be committed to faithful men able to teach others. The dictionary commends the ministry of preserving and spreading sound doctrine in print as a faithful application of the command to buy the truth and sell it not. As with any publisher, its books are to be read with discernment, weighed by Scripture, and not received uncritically merely for the imprint; but the Banner's great and abiding service has been to display the banner of truth in an age of doctrinal famine—keeping before the church the rich, God-centred, experimental divinity of the Reformation and Puritan heritage, that a new generation might recover the old paths.

pos: proper noun (the Low Countries under Spain)
etymology: The Low Countries under the rule of Catholic Habsburg Spain in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries; the arena of the Dutch Revolt and the Reformation's costly advance.
biblical_def: The Spanish Netherlands were the Low Countries (modern Netherlands and Belgium) under the rule of Catholic Habsburg Spain in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries—the arena of the Dutch Revolt and of the Reformation's costly advance against fierce persecution. As the Reformed faith spread through the provinces, the Spanish crown, under Charles V and Philip II, sought to crush it by the Inquisition, the edicts against heresy, and the sword. The Duke of Alva's “Council of Blood” executed thousands; whole congregations suffered for the gospel; and the resulting revolt, led by William of Orange, eventually won independence for the Protestant northern provinces (the Dutch Republic), while the southern provinces remained Catholic under Spain. Out of this furnace came the Belgic Confession, written by Guido de Brès, himself later martyred, and the Synod of Dort. The dictionary marks the Spanish Netherlands as a solemn theatre of the truth that the church is often born and preserved through blood, and of the providence of God over the rise and fall of nations. The Revelation's vision of the woman drunken with the blood of the saints was read by the Reformed of the persecuting power that slew them; and the Lord's beatitude rested on those persecuted for righteousness' sake. Yet the same God who permitted the persecution restrained and overruled it, for the king's heart is in His hand, and surely the wrath of man shall praise Him, the remainder of wrath He shall restrain. The Spanish Netherlands witness that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church, and that no empire, however mighty, can finally quench the truth God has resolved to preserve.

Secular history reduces the Dutch Revolt to a tale of taxes, trade, and political independence; the dictionary affirms the political dimension but denies the reduction. At its heart the struggle in the Spanish Netherlands was over the gospel: the Reformed faith spread, Catholic Spain sought to crush it by Inquisition and sword, and thousands suffered for righteousness' sake. The Reformed read in the woman drunken with the blood of the saints the persecuting power that slew them, and the Lord's beatitude rested on the persecuted.

The dictionary holds the Spanish Netherlands as a witness that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church, and that no empire, however mighty, can finally quench the truth God has resolved to preserve.

etymology: Latin Pudens, “modest, shamefast”; a believer at Rome who, with others, sent greeting to Timothy in Paul's last epistle (2 Timothy 4:21).
biblical_def: Pudens was a believer at Rome who, with Eubulus, Linus, Claudia, and the brethren, sent greeting to Timothy in the closing words of Paul's last epistle: “Eubulus greeteth thee, and Pudens, and Linus, and Claudia, and all the brethren.” Scripture tells us nothing more of him than this single, tender mention; yet the mention is precious. It comes from the apostle in his final imprisonment, awaiting martyrdom, when most had forsaken him—a glimpse of the small company of the faithful who stood by Paul and by the gospel in Rome at the end. The dictionary marks Pudens, with the others named, as a witness to two truths. First, the honour God gives to obscure and faithful saints: a man of whom we know nothing but his name and his presence among the brethren is nonetheless written in the inspired Word and, more, in the Lamb's book of life, for God is not unrighteous to forget the work and labour of love of His people. Not many wise or noble are called, yet the names of the faithful, however lowly, are remembered before God. Second, the existence of a believing fellowship in Rome—ordinary saints, some perhaps of Caesar's household—who comforted the imprisoned apostle. Later tradition wove legends about Pudens and Claudia (making them husband and wife, or linking them to Britain), but Scripture is silent, and the dictionary rests in what is written: a faithful brother, named by the Spirit, who stood with Paul and is remembered for ever. The least-known saint, faithful to the end, is not forgotten by God.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour God gives the obscure and faithful saint. Pudens is named once, and we know nothing of him but his name and his presence among the brethren who stood by Paul at the end. The world discounts such a man as insignificant; Scripture writes his name, and the Lamb's book of life holds it for ever, for God is not unrighteous to forget the labour of love of His people. Not many noble are called, yet the lowliest faithful name is remembered before God. The dictionary holds up Pudens as a comfort to every unknown saint: faithfulness, not fame, is what God records.

A lesser caution attends the legends. Where Scripture is silent, the church need not speculate; it is enough that the name is written by God, and that the faithful, however obscure, are not forgotten by Him.

etymology: Greek/Latin Linus; a believer at Rome who greeted Timothy with Paul (2 Timothy 4:21), traditionally reckoned an early leader of the Roman church.
biblical_def: Linus was a believer at Rome who, with Eubulus, Pudens, Claudia, and the brethren, sent greeting to Timothy in the last chapter of Paul's final epistle. As with Pudens, Scripture tells us nothing more than his name and his presence among the faithful at Rome in the apostle's closing days. Early tradition reckons this Linus to be the same who served as a leading elder or “bishop” of the church at Rome after the apostles—and Rome later placed him in its list of popes as the immediate successor of Peter. The dictionary marks Linus chiefly as another of the obscure faithful whom God names and remembers, whose name is written in the Word and in the book of life, though not many wise or noble are called. But it also marks the abuse made of his name. The mere appearance of Linus as an early Roman elder, even if the tradition be granted, gives no warrant for the developed papal claims later read back upon him. That a faithful man led the church at Rome in the first century is no proof of a monarchical papacy or of Roman primacy over the universal church; the New Testament knows a plurality of elders in each congregation, not a single supreme bishop ruling all. The dictionary therefore honours Linus as a faithful saint and an early servant of the Roman church, while refusing the inference that his name validates the papal succession Rome built upon it. The truth of Linus is the simple, precious one of 2 Timothy 4:21: a brother who stood with Paul and whose name God has not forgotten.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours Linus as another of the obscure faithful whom God names and remembers—a brother who stood with Paul at the end, whose name is written in the inspired Word and, by grace, in the Lamb's book of life. Not many wise or noble are called, yet God will not blot the faithful name out of His book but confess it before the Father. The simple, precious truth of 2 Timothy 4:21 is that a faithful man named Linus stood with the imprisoned apostle.

The corruption attaches to the use Rome has made of his name. Granting even the tradition that this Linus led the church at Rome after the apostles, the dictionary denies the inference built upon it: that an early Roman elder proves a monarchical papacy and the primacy of Rome over the universal church. The New Testament knows a plurality of elders in each congregation, not one supreme bishop ruling all; an early leading elder at Rome is no pope. The dictionary therefore honours Linus as a faithful early servant of the Roman church while refusing the papal-succession claims later read back upon him—for the validity of an office is the gospel preached, not a name on a list.

etymology: Hebrew Pir'athon; a town in the hill country of Ephraim, home of Abdon the judge and of one of David's mighty men.
biblical_def: Pirathon was a town in the hill country of Ephraim, in the region called the mount of the Amalekites, known in Scripture as the home of two faithful men. The first is Abdon the son of Hillel, the Pirathonite, who judged Israel after Elon, of whom it is recorded that he had forty sons and thirty nephews that rode on threescore and ten ass colts, and that he died and was buried in Pirathon. The second is Benaiah the Pirathonite, named among David's mighty men and set over a course of the army—a man of the same town who rose to serve the LORD's anointed in war. The dictionary notes Pirathon chiefly to ground the sacred history in real and traceable geography, and for the quiet witness of its men. Abdon belongs to the line of the minor judges, of whom Scripture records little beyond their names, families, and burial—yet they too were raised up of God to deliver and govern His people in the days when there was no king in Israel. Benaiah the Pirathonite stands among the valiant who gathered to David, the obscure faithful who served the kingdom of God's anointed. The dictionary marks the lesson that God uses men of small and unremarked towns for His purposes, and that the brief notices of the minor judges and the mighty men are not idle: they record real servants of God in their generations, and witness that the Lord raised up deliverers and warriors for His people from every quarter of the land, that His covenant purpose might go forward through the obscure as well as the great.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God works through obscure men and unremarked places. The brief notices of the minor judges—Abdon of Pirathon among them, of whom little is recorded but his family and his burial—are easily dismissed by the modern reader as idle genealogy. The dictionary answers that these were real deliverers raised up of God to govern His people when there was no king in Israel, and that their names are written in the inspired record. The Lord uses men of small towns; the history of redemption runs through the obscure as truly as the great.

Pirathon also grounds the sacred narrative in real geography. Skeptical readers treat the place-names of Judges and Samuel as legend; the dictionary affirms them as genuine towns of a real land, traceable in the hill country of Ephraim. From this one small town came both a judge of Israel and one of David's mighty men—a quiet witness that God raised up deliverers and warriors for His people from every quarter, that His covenant purpose might go forward. The least-noticed servant in the least-noticed town is part of the story God is telling.

etymology: Hebrew Bilhah, perhaps “timid” or “tender”; the handmaid of Rachel, given to Jacob, who bore Dan and Naphtali.
biblical_def: Bilhah was the handmaid of Rachel, given by her to Jacob as a wife when Rachel was barren, that she might “have children by her.” Bilhah bore Jacob two sons, Dan and Naphtali, who became heads of two of the twelve tribes of Israel. Her story belongs to the troubled, polygamous household of Jacob, where the rivalry of Leah and Rachel and the giving of their handmaids produced the twelve sons amid much strife—a household the LORD nevertheless used to build the nation of Israel. Bilhah is named again in the dark notice that Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, lay with her, defiling his father's bed—a sin for which Reuben forfeited the dignity of the firstborn, as Jacob declared on his deathbed: “Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel; because thou wentest up to thy father's bed.” The dictionary marks Bilhah's account for two sober lessons. First, it witnesses to the disorder and grief that attended the polygamy of the patriarchs—a practice Scripture records without commending, and which the LORD permitted in that age while His creation design of one man and one wife stood from the beginning. The tangled household of Jacob, with its rival wives and concubines, is a study in the bitterness that departure from the creation ordinance breeds. Second, it shows the sovereign grace of God, who built the twelve tribes—and so the line of promise—through a flawed and striving family, that the glory might be His and not man's. Bilhah's sons were no less tribes of Israel for their mother's lowly station; God's purpose ran through the household as it was, accomplishing His covenant through weak and sinful instruments.
webster_summary: Rachel's handmaid, given to Jacob, who bore Dan and Naphtali (Genesis 30:3-7); her account a witness to the grief of patriarchal polygamy and to the sovereign grace that built the twelve tribes through a flawed and striving household.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the distinction between what Scripture records and what it commends. The patriarchs' polygamy—Jacob with Leah, Rachel, and their handmaids Bilhah and Zilpah—is narrated honestly, with all its rivalry and grief, but never approved. The LORD permitted it in that age while His creation ordinance of one man and one wife stood from the beginning, and the bitter fruit of the tangled household witnesses against the departure from that design. The dictionary refuses the reading that takes the patriarchs' practice as God's endorsement; the narrative is a study in the strife that polygamy breeds, not a charter for it.

Bilhah's account also displays the sovereign grace of God, who built the twelve tribes—and the line of promise leading to Christ—through a flawed and striving family. Her sons Dan and Naphtali were no less tribes of Israel for their mother's lowly station as a handmaid. The dictionary marks the grace: God's covenant purpose ran through the household as it actually was, weak and sinful, accomplishing His design through instruments that gave Him no cause for boasting. That the nation of Israel rose from such a tangled house is a testimony that the glory of redemption belongs to God alone, who works His will through the unworthy.

etymology: Hebrew Makpelah, perhaps “double” (a double cave); the field and cave near Hebron that Abraham bought to bury Sarah, the burying-place of the patriarchs.
biblical_def: Machpelah was the field and cave near Mamre, in Hebron in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite as a burying-place for Sarah—the first piece of the promised land that the patriarch possessed. Though God had promised him the whole land, Abraham owned none of it in his lifetime save this grave; he insisted on buying it at full price, refusing it as a gift, that it might be a secure and lawful possession. There Sarah was buried, and afterward Abraham himself, and Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah, and at last Jacob, whose dying charge was that his sons carry his body up out of Egypt to lay him in the cave of Machpelah with his fathers. The dictionary marks Machpelah for its quiet but profound testimony of faith. Abraham's purchase of a grave in Canaan was an act of faith in the promise: he buried his dead in the land God had sworn to give his seed, declaring by that very act his confidence that the promise would stand though he himself died a stranger and pilgrim. So the writer to the Hebrews says of the patriarchs that they all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. Machpelah is the grave of pilgrims who looked for a better country—men who held the earthly land as the pledge of a heavenly inheritance, and who, dying in faith, were buried in hope of the resurrection and the city whose builder and maker is God.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the faith that buried its dead in the land of promise. A merely historical reading treats Machpelah as a property transaction—an old man buying a grave. Scripture frames it as an act of faith. God had promised Abraham the whole land, yet he owned none of it in his lifetime save this cave; and he insisted on buying it at full price, refusing it as a gift, that he might possess in Canaan a lawful pledge of the promise. To bury Sarah in the promised land was to confess that the promise would stand though he died a stranger in it.

So the patriarchs were laid one by one in Machpelah—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and their wives—and Jacob's dying charge to be carried up out of Egypt to that cave was a last confession of faith in the land God had sworn. The writer to the Hebrews gives the meaning: they all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off and embraced them, confessing themselves strangers and pilgrims on the earth, looking for a better country. The dictionary holds Machpelah as the grave of pilgrims who held the earthly land as the pledge of a heavenly inheritance, and who died in hope of the resurrection and the city whose builder and maker is God.

pos: noun phrase (the royal line of David)
etymology: From David and “line” (a lineage); the royal genealogy descending from David, through which the promised Messiah came, according to the covenant God made with David.
biblical_def: The Davidic line is the royal lineage descending from King David, through which the promised Messiah came, according to the covenant God made with David. When David purposed to build God a house, the LORD answered that He would instead build David a house, and swore: “Thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever.” This Davidic covenant promised an everlasting throne and an everlasting kingdom to David's seed—a promise that the failing succession of Judah's kings could never fulfil, but that found its yes in the greater Son of David. The prophets kept the hope alive through the line's decline: “there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots.” And the gospel opens by tracing it home: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham”; and the angel declared of Mary's son, “the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David… and of his kingdom there shall be no end.” The dictionary marks the Davidic line as a chief thread of the covenant of grace and a great proof of the faithfulness of God. Though the throne of Judah fell and the line sank to a stump, God preserved the lineage through exile and obscurity until the appointed Son was born, who reigns now at the Father's right hand and shall reign for ever. The dictionary holds the line against the rationalist denial of the messianic genealogies and against every scheme that severs the kingship of Christ from its Davidic root: Jesus is the Son of David, the heir of the everlasting throne, in whom the covenant with David is fulfilled and the kingdom established that shall never be destroyed.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the covenant faithfulness of God in the Davidic line. The rationalist treats the messianic genealogies of Matthew and Luke as later fabrications, contrived to fit Jesus into a royal pedigree. The dictionary affirms them as true records, traced under inspiration, fulfilling the covenant God swore to David of an everlasting throne. Though the kings of Judah failed and the throne fell, and the line sank to a stump in exile and obscurity, God preserved the lineage until the appointed Son was born—a proof that the word of the LORD cannot fail.

The opposite error severs the kingship of Christ from its Davidic root, treating His reign as a purely spiritual matter unconnected to the covenant promise. But the gospel insists on the connection: Jesus is the Son of David, the heir of the throne the LORD swore to establish for ever, and the angel declared He should receive the throne of His father David and reign over a kingdom without end. The dictionary holds the Davidic line as a chief thread of the covenant of grace: the everlasting throne promised to David is filled by his greater Son, who reigns now at the Father's right hand and shall reign for ever, the covenant kept and the kingdom established that shall never be destroyed.
